text.header: Most Common SE Types and Urgency
points: All types of epileptic seizures can evolve to SE, but the most commonly seen are GCSE, focal seizures without loss of consciousness (simple partial SE), myoclonic SE (MSE), and NCSE.
GCSE has the highest mortality and morbidity among all SE types and requires urgent and timely treatment.
Two operational time dimensions are defined:
t1: The time point at which a seizure is likely to be prolonged, leading to continuous seizure activity.
t2: The time of ongoing seizure activity beyond which there is a risk of long-term consequences (neuronal injury, death, network alteration, functional deficits).
Time points may vary between SE forms.
For convulsive (tonic-clonic) SE, time points are based on incomplete animal experiments and clinical research.

The division into two time points has clinical implications: t1 determines when treatment should be considered or started, and t2 determines treatment aggressiveness to prevent long-term consequences.
Tonic-clonic SE: t1 = 5 min, t2 = 30 min.
Focal SE with impaired consciousness: t1 = 10 min, t2 > 60 min.
Absence status epilepticus: t1 = 10–15 min, t2 = Unknown.

Known (symptomatic) causes can be acute (stroke, intoxication, CNS infection, trauma, metabolic), remote (posttraumatic, postencephalitic, poststroke), or progressive (brain tumor, dementia).

Sleep is a spontaneously recurring state of body and mind characterized by closed eyes, relaxed postural muscles, reduced interaction with the outside world, and decreased body movements.
Sleep is spontaneously reversible, differentiating it from coma.
Sleep has species-specific timing: nocturnal (active during the night) or diurnal (active during the day).
Sleep does not have a homogenous structure, with macrostructure divided into REM and NREM sleep.
REM and NREM sleep stages differ neurochemically, electrophysiologically, and neurobiologically.
NREM sleep is further divided into three substages: N1, N2, and N3.
* REM: “rapid eye movement”
Sleep stages include NREM stages (N1, N2, N3) and REM Stage (R).
Normal sleep has cyclic features where NREM and REM sleep stages follow each other regularly.
A healthy adult typically experiences 4-6 sleep cycles per night, with varying durations of NREM/REM and NREM stages within each cycle.

A hypnogram graphically demonstrates the variation of sleep stages during the night.
Percentages of sleep stages in a healthy adult:
Stage 1 NREM sleep: 2-5%
Stage 2 NREM sleep: 45-55%
Stage 3 NREM (deep) sleep: 15-20%
REM sleep: 20-25%
((Placeholder-5-1))
Sleep normally begins with NREM sleep; REM-onset sleep (within the first 15 minutes) is considered pathological.
After going to bed, sleep typically starts within 15-20 minutes with stage N1, a short transitional period.
Stage N2 usually begins within minutes, followed by deepening sleep to stage N3.
The first NREM sleep cycle evolves into REM sleep approximately 90-110 minutes after sleep onset.
The first half of the night is mainly constituted by deep sleep, while the second half features longer REM periods and decreased deep sleep percentages.

Rapid eye movements (REM) were discovered by Nathaniel Kleitman and Eugene Aserinsky in 1953 and were first associated with dreams.
Physiological changes during REM sleep include:
Rapid eye movements (saccadic, phasic, discrete, not associated with dream content).
Muscle atonia (continuous paralysis of skeletal muscles, except diaphragm and external eye muscles).
Desynchronized EEG activity (low amplitude, mixed frequency rapid activity resembling wakeful brain activity; also called paradoxical sleep).
Loss of thermoregulation (body temperature regulated by environmental temperature).
Cardiorespiratory irregularity (irregular heartbeats and respiration).
Nocturnal penile tumescence (NPT) (penile erection and clitoral engorgement).
Wakefulness and sleep are regulated by different brain regions and neurotransmitters.
Wake-related brain regions activating the cerebral cortex include the thalamus, basal forebrain, brainstem monoaminergic nuclei, and posterior hypothalamus.

NREM and REM sleep are regulated by different brain regions, including the ventrolateral preoptic (VLPO) neurons of the anterior hypothalamus and cholinergic neurons in the lateral dorsal tegmental/pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei.

The timing and duration of sleep, and timing of awakening, are regulated by the circadian clock and sleep homeostatic mechanisms.
The two-process model of sleep regulation incorporates Process S (homeostatic) and Process C (circadian).
Process S (homeostatic): Describes sleep pressure that increases during wakefulness and declines during sleep. Extended wakefulness leads to accumulated sleep pressure.

Process C (circadian): An internal clock regulating the organization of sleep and wake into specific phases of the day, synchronized by environmental cues like light, temperature, stress, exercise, food, and social interactions.
Wake-dependent homeostatic substances accumulate with wakefulness and promote sleep when sensed by a homeostatic system.
Suggested homeostatic substances include adenosine, cytokines (interleukin-1, tumor necrosis factor), prostaglandin D2, and nitric oxide.
Process S increases with prior waking duration, decreases during sleep, and shows predictable changes with naps.
Circadian-controlled processes are driven by an autonomously rhythmic system synchronized with environmental changes (e.g., light/dark cycle).
In mammals, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus orchestrates circadian timing of sleep/wake behavior, metabolism, and physiology.
The SCN projects mainly to other hypothalamic nuclei.

An urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by or caused by uncomfortable sensations.
Symptoms begin or worsen during rest, are relieved by movement, and occur predominantly in the evening or night.
Pathophysiology involves brain iron insufficiency and central nervous system dopamine dysregulation.
Early-onset RLS is often familial; late-onset RLS may be secondary to iron deficiency, pregnancy, or chronic renal failure.

Precipitating factors: Iron deficiency (serum ferritin < 50 μg/L), certain medications (sedating antihistamines, dopamine antagonists, most antidepressants except bupropion), pregnancy, chronic renal failure, prolonged immobility.
Treatment: Iron supplementation if ferritin < 75 μg/dl; medications include dopaminergic agents, antiepileptics, benzodiazepines, opiates, melatonin, and selegiline.

Treatment includes nonoperative measures like NSAIDs, physical therapy, and corticosteroid injections.
Arthroscopic subacromial decompression with possible acromioplasty is indicated for patients who fail conservative measures.

Ankle Sprains are common twisting injuries, the most frequent reason for missed athletic participation.
Diagnosis is clinical, with swelling, ecchymosis of the ankle, and pain with range of motion. Radiographs are indicated only when clinical examination meets criteria (Ottawa ankle rules).

[TYPE:Condition]Syndesmosis injury[/TYPE]: Damage to the ligamentous joint connecting the tibia and fibula in the lower leg, often associated with high ankle sprains.
[TYPE:Anatomy]ATFL (Anterior Talofibular Ligament)[/TYPE]: A primary ligament in the ankle that, when injured, characterizes a low ankle sprain.
[TYPE:Anatomy]CFL (Calcaneofibular Ligament)[/TYPE]: A ligament in the ankle often injured in conjunction with the ATFL during low ankle sprains.
[TYPE:Rule]Ottawa ankle rules[/TYPE]: A set of clinical criteria used to determine if radiographic examination is necessary for ankle or foot injuries.
Meningitis is defined as inflammation of the membranes of the brain or spinal cord (also known as arachnoiditis or leptomeningitis).
Encephalitis denotes inflammation of the brain itself.
Myelitis refers to inflammation of the spinal cord.
Combinations like meningoencephalitis or encephalomyelitis refer to more diffuse infection processes.
Abscesses are collections of infective and purulent material within the CNS ((Placeholder-3-1)) ((Placeholder-3-2)).
CNS infections can be caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and helminths.
Noninfectious etiologies that can mimic CNS infections include neoplastic diseases, intracranial tumors and cysts, medications, collagen vascular disorders, and other systemic illnesses.
The clinical presentation can be acute, subacute, or chronic, depending on the virulence of the infecting agent and the location of the infection.
CNS infections occur within the cranium or spinal column and may be associated with significant morbidity and mortality, often requiring emergent interventions.
The specific presentation depends on the pathogenesis of spread to the CNS, the virulence of the etiologic agent, and the area of CNS involvement.
Common clinical findings include fever, headache, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits, though these are nonspecific and not always present.
Acute meningitis typically presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status.
Patients with acute bacterial meningitis usually seek medical attention within hours to days of illness.
Nuchal rigidity ((Placeholder-9-1)), Kernig sign ((Placeholder-10-1)), and Brudzinski sign ((Placeholder-11-1)) are characteristic findings.
Presentation can vary with age, underlying conditions (head trauma, recent neurosurgery, CSF shunt, immunocompromised state), and the causative microorganism.

Common etiologic agents for acute meningitis include viruses (enteroviruses, HIV, mumps, herpes simplex) and bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes). Protozoa like Naegleria fowleri and Angiostrongylus cantonensis are less common.
Subacute or chronic meningitis presents over weeks to months or years, with a more gradual onset, lower fever, and potential lethargy and disability.

Causes of subacute or chronic meningitis include Mycobacteria (especially Mycobacterium tuberculosis), Spirochetes (Treponema pallidum, Borrelia burgdorferi), and Fungi (Cryptococcus neoformans, Coccidioides spp.). Patients with these infections are often immunocompromised.
Cryptococcal meningitis presentation differs in AIDS patients (more subtle, headache, lethargy) versus non-AIDS patients (subacute, headache, fever, meningismus, personality changes).
Acute encephalitis shares features with acute meningitis, often presenting with fever, headache, and altered mental status.
Mental status changes occur early due to diffuse involvement of the cerebral cortex.
Other findings include behavioral and speech disturbances, focal or diffuse neurologic signs (e.g., seizures, hemiparesis).

Viral causes like Herpes simplex virus can affect the CNS focally (temporal lobe), leading to personality changes, altered mentation, decreasing consciousness, seizures, and focal neurologic findings.

Other viral causes include Varicella-zoster virus, Cytomegalovirus, Human Herpesvirus 6, Arboviruses (West Nile, Eastern equine, St. Louis, California, Japanese encephalitis viruses), HIV, Rabies virus, and Enteroviruses.
Seasonality can suggest the agent (Arboviruses in summer/fall; HSV and HIV sporadically).
Non-viral causes include L. monocytogenes, Rickettsia spp., Ehrlichia spp., Bartonella spp., Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Toxoplasma gondii (especially in transplant patients).
Epidemiologic clues like geographic locale, local disease prevalence, travel history, occupational exposure, insect/animal contact, vaccination history, and immune status are helpful.
In many cases (32% to 75%), the etiology remains unknown despite testing.
Focal CNS lesions include brain abscess, subdural empyema, and epidural abscess.
Presentation depends on the route of spread, lesion location, and severity of increased intracranial pressure (ICP).
Brain abscesses can result from contiguous spread (sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis), trauma, or hematogenous dissemination.
Initial manifestations include headache, nausea, vomiting, and focal neurologic findings.
Seizures or altered consciousness may occur; fever is seen in less than 50% of patients.
Fungal brain abscesses (Aspergillus spp., Mucorales) can present as stroke syndromes due to vascular invasion.
Focal infections compressing the spinal cord can cause back pain, radiculopathy, motor and sensory deficits, potentially progressing to irreversible paralysis without emergency intervention.
LP is an essential diagnostic procedure for many CNS infections, especially those presenting with meningitis or encephalitis.
Normal CSF: 140-150 ml/day production, clear and colorless, no red or white blood cells, pressure 50-195 mm/H2O, glucose 40-80 mg/dl, protein 15-45 mg/dl, negative Gram stain and culture.
The spinal needle is typically inserted between the L3 and L4 vertebrae.

Complications range from mild discomfort to life-threatening conditions like headache (most common), infections, local bleeding, and brain herniation (most feared) ((Placeholder-32-1)). ((Placeholder-47-1))

General guidelines for LP without neuroimaging: age < 60, immunocompetent, no history of CNS disease, no recent seizure (< 1 week), normal sensorium/cognition, no papilledema, no focal neurologic deficits.

Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) is recommended before LP in patients with suspected intracranial mass lesion, immunocompromised state, history of CNS disease, new-onset seizure, abnormal consciousness, papilledema, focal neurologic deficit, or abnormal ocular motility.

Normal CSF opening pressure is 50-195 mm H2O. CSF is normally clear and colorless but can appear cloudy/turbid with increased WBCs (>200/mm³), RBCs (>400/mm³), bacteria (>10⁵ CFU/mL), or elevated protein (>2000 mg/dl).
Xanthochromia (yellow/yellow-orange supernatant) usually results from RBC lysis but can also occur with elevated CSF protein (>150 mg/dL) or systemic hyperbilirubinemia (>10-15 mg/dL).

CSF Findings in Meningitis: Viral (50-1000 WBC, Mononuclear, Glucose >45, Protein <200), Bacterial (1000-5000+ WBC, Neutrophil, Glucose <40, Protein 100-500), Tuberculosis (50-300 WBC, Mononuclear, Glucose <45, Protein 50-300), Cryptococcal (20-500 WBC, Mononuclear, Glucose <40, Protein >45).
Cultures are important for identifying the etiologic agent. CSF Gram stain provides clues. India ink is positive in 50-75% of cryptococcal meningitis. PCR tests are highly sensitive and specific.
Rapid administration of bactericidal antibiotics with good CNS and tissue penetration is crucial.
Empiric antibiotic choice is based on broad-spectrum coverage of common pathogens, considering local prevalence.
Recommendations often include ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, and vancomycin for optimal coverage of resistant organisms.
High-dose ampicillin is added if Listeria is suspected (young/old, immunocompromised).
For penicillin/cephalosporin allergy, meropenem or chloramphenicol plus vancomycin are recommended.
Delay in antibiotic administration is associated with worsening outcomes; diagnostic tests should not delay empiric therapy.
Dexamethasone is recommended in adults, given before or with initial antibiotics and continued for 4 days.

Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for high-risk exposures to Neisseria or Hib meningitis (household contacts, exposure to oral secretions, intubation without a mask). Regimens include ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, or rifampin.
Prophylaxis is not indicated for pneumococcal meningitis.
Only HSV disease has specific therapy (Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours).
Ganciclovir can be used for CMV infections.
Pleconaril shows promise for enteroviral disease.
Symptomatic treatment is generally provided.
Treatment involves appropriate antibiotics and neurosurgical consultation.
Antibiotic choice should consider likely pathogens (especially anaerobes) and CSF penetration, often including a third-generation cephalosporin and metronidazole.
Vancomycin is often added for recently postoperative patients.
Drainage may be necessary.

[TYPE:Condition]Encephalomyelitis[/TYPE]: A condition involving inflammation of both the brain and the spinal cord.

[TYPE:Sign]Nuchal rigidity[/TYPE]: Stiffness of the neck, preventing flexion, a characteristic sign of meningitis.

[TYPE:Sign]Brudzinski sign[/TYPE]: A sign of meningitis where passive flexion of the neck causes involuntary flexion of the knees and hips.

Most episodes of fever are short-lived and do not require diagnostic investigation or specific therapy.
Some fevers can be readily diagnosed and effectively treated.
A small but important subgroup of fevers are persistent and difficult to diagnose.
Puzzling fevers have fascinated and frustrated clinicians since the earliest days of clinical studies.
Prolonged and Perplexing Fevers (Keefer and Leard, 1955) and Fever of Unknown Origin: Report on 100 cases (Petersdorf and Beeson, 1961) are historical references.
In the United States, 'fever of unknown origin (FUO)' is generally used.
In other countries, 'pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO)' is often used.

The first formal definition by Petersdorf and Beeson (nearly five decades ago) included: fever higher than 38.3° C, persisting without diagnosis for at least 3 weeks, and persisting after at least 1 week of investigation in hospital.
Investigators have modified and extended this definition to include Classical FUO, Health Care Associated FUO, Immune-deficient FUO, and HIV-related FUO.

Advances like computed axial tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound imaging, nucleic acid-based diagnostic testing, and rapid tests for pathogens have changed the landscape of FUO diagnosis.
Classical FUO: >38.0° C, >3 weeks, >2 visits or 3 days in hospital. Leading causes: Cancer, infections, inflammatory conditions, undiagnosed habitual hyperthermia.
Health care-associated FUO: >38.0° C, >3 days, not present or incubating on admission. Causes: Health care-associated infections, postoperative complications, drug fever.
Immune-Deficient FUO: >38.0° C, >3 days, negative cultures after 48 hr. Causes: Majority due to infections (40%-60% documented).

HIV-Related FUO: 38.0° C, >3 weeks for outpatients, >3 days for inpatients, confirmed HIV infection. Causes: HIV (primary infection), typical and atypical mycobacteria, CMV, lymphomas, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
Most patients with classical FUO have subacute or chronic symptoms and can be safely investigated as outpatients.
In one series, the median duration of fever before diagnosis was 40 days.
Disorders causing classical FUO fall into five categories: Infections, Neoplasms, Connective tissue diseases, Miscellaneous other disorders, and Undiagnosed illnesses.

text.header: Infections as a Cause of Classical FUO
points: Infections are the largest category, accounting for 25% to 50% of cases.
In patients over 65 years, infections become less common, falling to second or third place.
Consistently important infections include abscesses, endocarditis, tuberculosis, and complicated urinary tract infections.
Incidence of infections varies by locale (e.g., visceral leishmaniasis in Spain, familial Mediterranean fever in Ashkenazi Jews, Kikuchi’s disease in Japan, TRAPS in Ireland).

Rare causes include Addison’s disease, Adult Still’s disease, Alcoholic hepatitis, Aortic dissection, Behçet’s syndrome, Chronic meningitis, Erythema multiforme, Fabry’s disease, Granulomatous hepatitis, Histiocytosis X, Inflammatory bowel disease, Pheochromocytoma, Sarcoidosis, Vitamin B12 deficiency, and others.

Other miscellaneous causes include Allergic alveolitis, Atrial myxoma, Autoimmune cholangitis, Bartonellosis, Carcinomatous meningitis, Castleman’s disease, Cirrhotic fever, Cyclic neutropenia, Drug fever and other Hypersensitivities, Factitious fever, Familial Hibernian fever, Familial Mediterranean fever, Giant coronary aneurysm, Granulomatous peritonitis, Hantavirus infection, Hemoglobinopathies, Hemolytic anemias, Hemophagocytic syndrome, Human picornavirus infection, Hypereosinophilic syndrome, Immunoblastic lymphadenopathy, Infected urachal cyst, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, Lofgren syndrome, Lymphomatoid granulomatosis, Metal fume fever, Myeloproliferative syndromes, Pancreatitis, Parathyroid apoplexy, Paroxysmal hemoglobinurias, Pericarditis, Periodic fever, Polyarteritis nodosa, Postpericardiotomy syndrome, Pulmonary emboli, Resorbing hematoma, Retroperitoneal fibrosis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, Schnitzler’s syndrome, Sinusitis, Serum sickness, Sjögren’s syndrome, Subacute necrotizing lymphadenitis, Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, Thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, Veno-occlusive disease, Wegener’s granulomatosis, and Whipple’s disease.

text.header: Connective Tissue Diseases in Classical FUO
points: Connective tissue diseases like Still’s disease (juvenile rheumatoid arthritis), other variants of rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus predominate in younger patients.
Temporal arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica syndromes are more common in elderly patients.
Malignant neoplasms can induce fever directly through pyrogenic cytokines (lymphomas).
They can also generate fevers indirectly through spontaneous or induced necrosis or by creating conditions for secondary infections, such as postobstructive pneumonia.

text.header: Classical FUO in Infants and Children
points: Diseases causing classical FUO in infants differ from those in older children and adults.
Respiratory infections cause classical FUO in infants more often than in children over 12 months or adults.
Infections are frequent causes in infants, while connective tissue diseases and cancers are rare.
Kawasaki disease occurs in children younger than 5 years.
Connective tissue diseases are rarely seen in children younger than 12 months.
Still’s disease is a leading cause of FUO in older children and young adults.
Joint involvement in children with FUO can signify serious underlying disorders like connective tissue disease, endocarditis, or leukemia.
In a series of 146 pediatric cases, a specific diagnosis was established in 84 (57.5%).
Diagnoses included: 64 (43.8%) Infections, 11 (7.5%) Autoimmune disorders, 4 (2.7%) Malignant neoplasms, and 5 (3.4%) other disorders (drug-induced fever, sarcoidosis, mercury poisoning).
Most common infectious diseases diagnosed were Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (15%), Osteomyelitis (10%), Bartonellosis (5%), and Urinary tract infections (4%).
In patients over 65 years, connective tissue diseases are frequently identified as the cause of FUO, surpassing infections as the leading cause in developed countries.
Temporal arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica syndromes are common in the elderly.
Infections identified in elderly patients include intra-abdominal abscesses, complicated urinary tract infections, tuberculosis, and endocarditis.
For patients <65 years (n=152): Infections 35%, Tumors 5%, Multisystem diseases 17%, Miscellaneous 26%, No diagnosis 29%.
For patients >65 years (n=201): Infections 21%, Tumors 19%, Multisystem diseases 28%, Miscellaneous 8%, No diagnosis 9%.
Fever in returned travelers is most often due to common infections like Malaria, Respiratory tract Infections, and Urinary tract infections.
Health care-associated FUO occurs when patients manifest fever during active medical treatment for another illness.
Risk factors include surgical procedures, urinary and respiratory tract instrumentation, intravascular devices, drug therapy, and immobilization.
Immunosuppressed patients have the highest incidence of FUO.
In patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity, FUO is often due to infections (58%), non-infectious causes (25%), or undetermined (17%).
Neutropenia, resulting from cytotoxic therapy or malignancies affecting the bone marrow, is a dangerous condition and a special subclass of immunodeficiency.
Fever episodes are common in neutropenia, often short-lived due to rapid response to treatment or rapidly fatal infections.
Bacteremia and sepsis are frequent causes; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered promptly.
About 35% of prolonged febrile neutropenia episodes respond to broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy.

If fever does not respond promptly to antibacterial therapy, fungal infection, resistant bacterial infections, tuberculosis, Toxoplasma gondii, Graft-Versus-Host disease, drug fever, or toxic effects of chemotherapy must be considered.
The primary phase of HIV infection is characterized by a mononucleosis-like illness with prominent fever.
During the long subclinical infection period, patients are usually afebrile.
In later phases of untreated HIV infection, fever episodes become common, often signifying superimposed opportunistic infections.

Evaluation typically includes a comprehensive history, verification of fever, consideration of fever pattern, repeated physical examinations, laboratory investigations, imaging studies, and invasive diagnostic procedures.

History is crucial for guiding initial laboratory investigations, with attention to recent travel, animal exposure, work environment, contact with similar symptoms, family history, past medical history, and obtained medications.
Verification of fever is important, as up to 35% of patients investigated for prolonged fever were found not to have significant fever or to have factitious fever.
Fever patterns include Febris continue, Febris recurrens, Intermittent (Hectic), Febris undulens (Pel-Ebstein), Remittent, and Subfebril fever.
Pulse-temperature disassociation can be seen in typhoid fever and atypical pneumonia (1-degree fever elevation with 20 heartbeats elevation).

Key physical abnormalities in FUO can be subtle and require repeated examinations (e.g., nodular temporal artery in temporal arteritis, oral ulcers in histoplasmosis or Behçet’s syndrome, choroid granuloma or epididymal nodule in extrapulmonary tuberculosis, testicular nodule in polyarteritis nodosa, rectal fluctuance of a perirectal abscess).

Physical findings by body site can suggest diagnoses: Sinus tenderness (Sinusitis), Nodules/reduced pulsation of temporal artery (Temporal arteritis), Ulceration of oropharynx (Histoplasmosis), Tender tooth (Periapical abscess), Choroid tubercle in fundus (Disseminated granulomatosis), Petechiae/Roth spots in conjunctiva (Endocarditis), Enlargement/tenderness of thyroid (Thyroiditis), Murmur (Infective endocarditis), LAP/Splenomegaly in abdomen (Lymphoma, endocarditis, disseminated granulomatosis), Perirectal fluctuance (Abscess), Testicular nodule (Periarteritis nodosa), Epididymal nodule (Disseminated granulomatosis), Deep venous tenderness in lower extremities (Thrombosis, thrombophlebitis), Petechiae, clubbing, splinter hemorrhages, subcutaneous nodule on skin/nails (Vasculitis, endocarditis).
Noninvasive laboratory tests yield diagnoses in approximately a quarter of cases.
Most useful tests include serologic tests, blood smears, and microbial cultures.
Bone marrow examination is considered for suspected granulomatous diseases (Tuberculosis, Histoplasmosis, Sarcoidosis, Carcinomatosis, Hemophagocytic syndrome).

Imaging studies include Ultrasound (USG), Computed tomography (CT), Magnetic resonance imaging (MR), Scanning with labeled autologous leukocytes, Gallium 67 scanning, and Positron emission tomography (PET).
Histopathologic examination of tissues obtained by excisional biopsy, needle biopsy, laparoscopy, or laparotomy can provide answers, but yields the final diagnosis in less than half of FUO patients.
The diagnostic yield of operative and CT-guided biopsies is higher than bedside procedures.
Exploratory laparotomy is rarely performed today unless localized abdominal signs or imaging findings are present, as CT scanning or MRI rarely miss abdominal abnormalities.
((Placeholder-50-1)) ((Placeholder-40-1)) ((Placeholder-58-1))
Empirical therapy with anti-inflammatory agents (corticosteroids, aspirin), antimicrobial agents, or antineoplastic drugs was used in the past but is seldom indicated today.

Limitations and risks of empirical trials include spontaneous remission giving a false impression of success and the nonspecific action of drugs (e.g., Rifampin against various bacteria, naproxen for malignant neoplasms).
Therapeutic trials, even if successful in reducing fever, may delay correct diagnosis and appropriate treatment.
A fundamental principle is to withhold therapy until the cause of fever is determined, allowing for tailored treatment.
For febrile neutropenic patients, principles differ: broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy should be administered immediately after obtaining culture samples.
Elderly patients with malignant neoplasms have the poorest prognosis.
Diagnostic delay adversely affects prognosis in intra-abdominal infections, miliary tuberculosis, disseminated fungal infections, and recurrent pulmonary emboli.

Comprehensive history, repeated physical examinations, complete blood count, routine blood chemistry, urinalysis, chest radiograph, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, blood cultures (three or more separate specimens without antimicrobial therapy), Cytomegalovirus IgM antibodies or viral detection, Heterophile antibody test (in children/young adults), Tuberculin skin test, CT of abdomen/pelvis/other sites, MRI, Radionuclide scans, HIV antibodies or viral detection assay, further evaluation of any abnormality, and Venous duplex imaging of lower limbs.

[TYPE:Condition]Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO)[/TYPE]: A condition characterized by persistent fever that remains undiagnosed after a specified period of investigation.
[TYPE:Condition]Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO)[/TYPE]: An alternative term used in some countries for Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO).
[TYPE:Measurement]Temperature Threshold[/TYPE]: A specific body temperature, typically higher than 38.0° C or 38.3° C, used as a criterion in the definition of FUO.
[TYPE:Timeframe]Diagnostic Duration[/TYPE]: The minimum period of fever, usually at least 3 weeks, required to meet the definition of FUO.
[TYPE:Setting]Health Care Associated FUO[/TYPE]: A subtype of FUO occurring in patients receiving medical care, with fever developing after a certain period of hospitalization or treatment.
[TYPE:Condition]Immune-Deficient FUO[/TYPE]: A subtype of FUO specifically defined for patients with compromised immune systems, often with a shorter duration criterion.
[TYPE:Condition]HIV-Related FUO[/TYPE]: A subtype of FUO defined for patients with confirmed HIV infection, with specific duration criteria for outpatients and inpatients.
[TYPE:Category]Classical FUO[/TYPE]: The traditional subtype of FUO defined by prolonged fever, typically without a clear cause after initial investigations.
[TYPE:Category]Infections[/TYPE]: A major category of causes for FUO, accounting for a significant percentage of diagnosed cases.
[TYPE:Category]Neoplasms[/TYPE]: Cancers and other malignant growths that can present as a cause of FUO.
[TYPE:Category]Connective Tissue Diseases[/TYPE]: A group of autoimmune disorders affecting connective tissues, which can lead to FUO.
[TYPE:Disease]Tuberculosis[/TYPE]: An infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, frequently identified as a cause of FUO.
[TYPE:Disease]Endocarditis[/TYPE]: Inflammation of the inner lining of the heart, often caused by infection, and a notable cause of FUO.
[TYPE:Disease]Temporal Arteritis[/TYPE]: Inflammation of arteries, particularly in the head, more common in the elderly and a cause of FUO.
[TYPE:Disease]Polymyalgia Rheumatica[/TYPE]: An inflammatory condition causing muscle pain and stiffness, often associated with temporal arteritis in the elderly.
[TYPE:Disease]Kawasaki Disease[/TYPE]: An illness causing inflammation in blood vessels throughout the body, primarily affecting children younger than 5 years.
[TYPE:Disease]Still's Disease[/TYPE]: A form of inflammatory arthritis, also known as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, a leading cause of FUO in older children and young adults.
[TYPE:Process]Neutropenia[/TYPE]: A condition characterized by an abnormally low level of neutrophils, increasing susceptibility to infection and complicating FUO diagnosis.
[TYPE:Diagnostic Tool]Wood's Lamp[/TYPE]: A device emitting ultraviolet light used to examine the skin, sometimes employed in FUO investigations.
[TYPE:Diagnostic Procedure]Excisional Biopsy[/TYPE]: A surgical procedure to remove a tissue sample for examination, used in invasive diagnostic procedures for FUO.
Osteoporosis is a disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, leading to enhanced bone fragility and an increased fracture incidence.
According to the WHO, osteoporosis is defined as a BMD T-score of -2.5 or less ((Placeholder-2-1)) ((Placeholder-2-2)). ((Placeholder-1-1)) ((Placeholder-1-2)) ((Placeholder-1-3))
Trabecular bone and bone quality are not the sole factors in fracture occurrence ((Placeholder-3-1)) ((Placeholder-3-2)) ((Placeholder-3-3)) ((Placeholder-3-4)). ((Placeholder-1-4))

Factors contributing to fracture risk include bone mass, bone structure, bone quality, fall risk, impact of fall, skeletal strength, type of fall, energy reduction, external protection, neuromuscular function, environmental risks, and age ((Placeholder-4-1)).
Risk factors for osteoporosis include female sex, sedentary lifestyle, multiple births, and excessive alcohol use ((Placeholder-5-1)) ((Placeholder-5-2)) ((Placeholder-5-3)) ((Placeholder-5-4)).
Osteoporosis affects approximately 8 million women in the US, with 22 million women having osteopenia.
The risk of fragility fractures includes 250,000 hip fractures and 500,000 vertebral fractures per year in women ((Placeholder-6-1)).
Normal bone turnover involves osteoclasts for resorption and osteoblasts for formation and mineralization.
In osteoporosis, resorption exceeds formation.
Bone mass peaks by mid-30s, and bone loss begins several years prior to menopause.
The risk of fracture increases with BMD loss ((Placeholder-7-1)) ((Placeholder-7-2)) ((Placeholder-7-3)) ((Placeholder-7-4)) ((Placeholder-8-1)).
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is a screening method.
Femoral neck BMD is the best predictor of hip fractures.
Forearm BMD predicts non-hip fractures ((Placeholder-9-1)) ((Placeholder-9-2)) ((Placeholder-9-3)).

text.header: FRAX Tool for Fracture Risk Assessment
points: FRAX is a diagnostic tool used to evaluate the 10-year probability of bone fracture risk.

It integrates clinical risk factors and BMD at the femoral neck to calculate the 10-year probability of hip fracture and major osteoporotic fracture (clinical spine, forearm, hip, or shoulder fracture) ((Placeholder-10-1)) ((Placeholder-10-2)).
Senile osteoporosis is common, with some degree of osteopenia found in virtually all healthy elderly patients.
Treatable causes should be investigated, including nutritional deficiency, malabsorption syndromes, hyperparathyroidism, Cushing's disease, and tumors ((Placeholder-11-1)).
Morbidity and mortality are much higher in men than women with osteoporotic fractures.
Secondary causes are more common in men, accounting for 50%.
Androgens may inhibit bone resorption.
The average onset is 10 years later than in women, and men are often asymptomatic at onset ((Placeholder-12-1)) ((Placeholder-12-2)).
Age-standardized mortality ratios after proximal femur fractures are 2.2 in women and 3.2 in men.
For vertebral fractures, the ratios are 1.7 in women and 2.4 in men.
For other major fractures, the ratios are 1.9 in women and 2.2 in men.
For other minor fractures, the ratios are 0.8 in women and 1.5 in men ((Placeholder-13-1)).
Exercise includes muscle strengthening and gait training.
Orthotics such as supporters can be used.
Calcium (1000-1200 mg/day) and Vitamin D (600-800 IU/day) are important.
Antiresorptives include Estrogens/HRT, SERMs, Calcitonin, Bisphosphonates, and Denosumab.
Anabolic agents include PTH.

Strontium ranelate has dual action, increasing new bone deposition by osteoblasts and reducing osteoclast resorption ((Placeholder-14-1)) ((Placeholder-15-1)) ((Placeholder-16-1)) ((Placeholder-17-1)) ((Placeholder-18-1)) ((Placeholder-19-1)).

text.header: Common Fractures in Elderly Osteoporotic Patients
points: Hip Fractures: femoral neck, intertrochanteric, and subtrochanteric fractures.
Other common fractures include ankle fractures, proximal humerus fracture, distal radius fractures, and vertebral compression fractures ((Placeholder-20-1)).
Fractures in elderly osteoporotic patients present a challenge to orthopedic surgeons.
The goal of treatment is to restore the pre-injury level of function.

Fracture complications can disable elderly patients, affecting normal daily activities and independent mobilization ((Placeholder-21-1)) ((Placeholder-21-2)) ((Placeholder-21-3)) ((Placeholder-21-4)) ((Placeholder-21-5)) ((Placeholder-21-6)).
Osteopenia complicates both fracture treatment and healing.
Internal fixation is compromised due to poor screw purchase and increased risk of screw pull-out; locking screw-plate fixation and PMMA with endoprosthesis may be used.
There is an increased risk of non-union, and bone augmentation (bone graft, substitutes) may be indicated ((Placeholder-22-1)) ((Placeholder-22-2)) ((Placeholder-22-3)) ((Placeholder-22-4)).

Assessment includes medical history (pre-existing cardiac and pulmonary disease, diabetes), cognitive status (Alzheimer's, CVA, Parkinson's, senile dementia), and functional history (ambulatory status: community, household, non-functional, non-ambulator; living arrangements) ((Placeholder-23-1)) ((Placeholder-24-1)).
Hip fracture incidence increases after age 50, with a female:male ratio of 2:1.
Femoral neck and intertrochanteric fractures are seen with equal frequency.

Acne vulgaris is a self-limited disorder of the pilosebaceous unit primarily seen in adolescents.
It presents with a pleomorphic array of lesions: comedones, papules, pustules, and nodules.
While self-limiting, its sequelae can be lifelong, including pitted or hypertrophic scar formation.
((Placeholder-1-1))
Acne is common, often termed physiologic, and heralds the onset of puberty.
In girls, acne may precede menarche by over a year, with comedones being the predominant lesions in very young patients.
Acne prevalence peaks in mid-to-late teenage years, affecting over 85% of adolescents, and then steadily decreases.

The pathogenesis of acne is multifaceted, involving four basic steps: follicular epidermal hyperproliferation, excess sebum production, inflammation, and the presence and activity of Propionibacterium acnes.
Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation leads to the formation of a microcomedo due to hyperkeratosis and increased keratinocyte cohesion in the infundibulum.
Excess cells and tackiness create a plug in the follicular ostium, causing accumulation of keratin, sebum, and bacteria.
These packed concretions lead to dilation of the upper hair follicle, forming a microcomedo.
Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a potent androgen, may play a role in acne.
((Placeholder-6-1))
Lesions commonly appear on the face, back, chest, and shoulders.
Lesions can be noninflammatory (comedos: closed/whiteheads, open/blackheads) or inflammatory.
Open comedones appear as flat or slightly raised lesions with a dark, impacted follicular center.
Closed comedones are pale, slightly elevated small papules without a visible orifice.
Inflammatory lesions range from small papules with red borders to pustules and large, tender, fluctuant nodules.
Severe cases of inflammatory acne, previously termed nodulocystic, are now described as severe nodular acne, as true cysts are rare.
The appearance as a papule, pustule, or nodule depends on the extent and location of the inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis.

Scarring is a potential complication of acne.
Four general types of acne scars exist: ice pick (narrow, deep, tapering), rolling (shallow, wide, undulating), boxcar (wide, sharply demarcated), and hypertrophic (rare, especially on the trunk).
Acne vulgaris is usually an isolated cutaneous finding, except in cases of hyperandrogenism, which may present with hirsutism, precocious puberty, and other signs of androgen excess.

Elevated serum androgen levels may be found in severe cystic acne or acne associated with endocrine conditions like congenital adrenal hyperplasia, ovarian or adrenal tumors, and polycystic ovarian disease.
In most acne patients, serum androgens are within the normal range.
Specific tests include serum DHEAS, total testosterone, free testosterone, LH/FSH ratio, and serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone to identify adrenal sources of androgens when other sources are unclear.
Testing should be performed before or during the menstrual period, not midcycle.

Conditions to differentiate include Milia, Sebaceous hyperplasia, Dilated pore of Winer (Favre–Racouchot syndrome), Rosacea, Perioral dermatitis, Neonatal acne, Miliaria rubra, Pseudofolliculitis barbae, Acne keloidalis nuchae, Keratosis pilaris, and Neurotic excoriations/factitial.
Complications include transient macular erythema, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation (especially in darker skin types), scarring, and psychiatric disturbances.

text.header: Acne Vulgaris Prognosis and Clinical Course
points: Acne can start as early as 6-8 years of age or appear later in life (20s or beyond).
Most patients clear by their early twenties, but some experience acne into their thirties or forties.
In women, acne often fluctuates with the menstrual cycle, flaring just before menstruation, though this is not due to increased sebaceous gland activity in the luteal phase.
Prepubescent females with comedonal acne and those with high DHEAS levels are predictors of severe or long-standing nodulocystic acne.
Treatment involves cleansing and topical agents such as Sulfur/Sodium Sulfacetamide/Resorcinol, Salicylic Acid, Azelaic Acid, Benzoyl Peroxide, topical antibiotics, and retinoids.

Systemic therapy includes antibiotics (Tetracyclines, Macrolides, Trimethoprim–Sulfamethoxazole, Cephalexin, Clindamycin, Dapsone) and hormonal therapy (Oral Contraceptives, Glucocorticoids, Antiandrogens, Isotretinoin).
Benzoyl Peroxide is a topical treatment ((Placeholder-25-1)).
While milk, high-glycemic index foods, chocolate, sweets, and fatty foods are often discussed, there is no evidence to support the value of eliminating these foods.
Variants include Neonatal acne, Infantile acne, Acne conglobata, Acne fulminans, SAPHO Syndrome, PAPA Syndrome, Acne Excoriee des Jeunes Filles, and Acne Mechanica.
Rosacea is characterized by persistent erythema of the central face, typically affecting the nose, cheeks, chin, and forehead.
Primary features include flushing, papules, pustules, and telangiectases.
Secondary features can include facial burning or stinging, edema, plaques, dryness, phyma, peripheral flushing, and ocular manifestations.
Erythema in peripheral locations (scalp, ears, lateral face, neck, chest) can also occur.
The prevalence of rosacea is unknown, occurring mostly in fair-skinned populations.

Contributing factors may include facial vascular reactivity, dermal connective tissue structure, matrix composition, pilosebaceous structure, microbial colonization, or a combination of factors altering the cutaneous response to triggers.
Sun damage is considered a contributing factor, with solar elastosis often superimposed on rosacea histology.
Common triggers include hot or cold temperatures, sunlight, wind, hot drinks, exercise, spicy food, alcohol, emotions, cosmetics, topical irritants, and medications that promote flushing.
Menopausal flushing is also a trigger.

[TYPE:Condition]Acne vulgaris[/TYPE]: A self-limited disorder of the pilosebaceous unit, primarily affecting adolescents, characterized by comedones, papules, pustules, and nodules.
[TYPE:Anatomy]Pilosebaceous unit[/TYPE]: The anatomical structure consisting of a hair follicle and its associated sebaceous gland and arrector pili muscle.
[TYPE:Lesion]Comedone[/TYPE]: A noninflammatory lesion of acne, either open (blackhead) or closed (whitehead), caused by a plug of keratin and sebum in the follicular ostium.
[TYPE:Lesion]Papule[/TYPE]: A small, raised, inflammatory lesion of acne, typically red and tender.
[TYPE:Lesion]Pustule[/TYPE]: A small, raised, inflammatory lesion of acne containing pus, often with a red border.
[TYPE:Lesion]Nodule[/TYPE]: A large, tender, inflammatory lesion of acne, extending into the deeper layers of the skin.
[TYPE:Process]Hyperkeratosis[/TYPE]: Excessive thickening of the outer layer of the skin (stratum corneum), contributing to follicular plugging in acne.
[TYPE:Substance]Sebum[/TYPE]: An oily, waxy substance produced by sebaceous glands, which can accumulate in hair follicles.
[TYPE:Microorganism]Propionibacterium acnes[/TYPE]: A bacterium commonly found on the skin that plays a role in the pathogenesis of acne through inflammation.
[TYPE:Hormone]Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)[/TYPE]: A potent androgen hormone that may contribute to acne development by stimulating sebum production.
[TYPE:Scar]Ice pick scar[/TYPE]: A type of acne scar characterized by narrow, deep, and tapering V-shaped openings.
[TYPE:Scar]Rolling scar[/TYPE]: A type of acne scar with shallow, wide, and undulating depressions, giving the skin an uneven appearance.
[TYPE:Scar]Boxcar scar[/TYPE]: A type of acne scar with wide, sharply demarcated vertical walls, often round or oval.
[TYPE:Scar]Hypertrophic scar[/TYPE]: An elevated, raised scar that forms as a result of excessive collagen production during wound healing, less common in acne.
[TYPE:Condition]Hyperandrogenism[/TYPE]: A condition characterized by excessive levels of androgens, which can be associated with acne and other symptoms like hirsutism.
[TYPE:Condition]Rosacea[/TYPE]: A chronic inflammatory skin condition primarily affecting the central face, characterized by erythema, flushing, papules, pustules, and telangiectases.
[TYPE:Lesion]Telangiectasia[/TYPE]: Dilated small blood vessels visible on the skin surface, often a feature of rosacea.
[TYPE:Subtype]Erythematotelangiectatic Rosacea (ETR)[/TYPE]: A subtype of rosacea characterized by persistent facial erythema, flushing, and telangiectases.
[TYPE:Subtype]Papulopustular Rosacea[/TYPE]: A subtype of rosacea presenting with persistent central facial erythema accompanied by papules and pustules.
[TYPE:Subtype]Phymatous Rosacea[/TYPE]: A subtype of rosacea characterized by thickened skin, irregular contours, and nodularities, most commonly affecting the nose (rhinophyma).
